stages.title: Medical terminology
stages.hook: Gastroenteritis, nephritis, tachycardia: these long words look scary. Can you decode one even if you have never seen it?
explain: Medical words are built from parts, mostly from Greek and Latin. A word can have a prefix at the start, a root in the middle and a suffix at the end. Learn the parts and you can decode thousands of words.

Examples: cardi- means heart, nephr- means kidney, gastr- means stomach, hepat- means liver, pneumo- relates to lungs or air. The suffix -itis means inflammation, -ectomy means surgical removal, -ology means the study of, -pathy means disease.
Prefixes change meaning: tachy- fast, brady- slow, hyper- above or too much, hypo- below or too little, a- or an- without. So tachycardia is a fast heart rate and hypoglycaemia is low blood sugar.

steps: Nephr- refers to the kidney.
-itis means inflammation.
Put together: inflammation of the kidney.

analogies.home: Lego bricks snap together to make many models. Word parts snap together to make many terms.

analogies.music: Notes combine into chords. Roots, prefixes and suffixes combine into terms.
analogies.city: Street names such as North, Old and Bridge combine to name places. Word parts name conditions.

stages.mnemonic: Prefix-Root-Suffix: P-R-S, like a train with front, middle and back carriages.
terms: A word part at the start that changes the meaning.
The core word part, often a body part.
A word part at the end, such as -itis for inflammation.

misc.wrong: Medical terms have to be memorised one by one.
misc.right: Most are built from a small set of parts. Learn the parts and you can decode the whole word.

stages.title: Patient history-taking
stages.hook: A famous teaching saying is that listening to the patient gives most of the diagnosis. What should you ask to hear the whole story?
explain: The history is the patient's story, and it is often the most useful clue in medicine. A typical order is: introduction, presenting complaint, history of the presenting complaint, past medical history, medications, allergies, family history, social history and a review of other systems.

For a symptom such as pain, one useful set of questions is SOCRATES: Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associated symptoms, Time course, Exacerbating or relieving factors, Severity. Start with open questions ('Tell me about it') and then use closed ones to fill gaps.

Always ask about allergies and current medicines, including herbal and over-the-counter ones. Ask about red flags. Ask in a way that respects privacy and culture. If a patient cannot speak for themself, a family member or carer may add the story.

example.q: A fictional patient says 'I have a pain in my tummy'. Which questions come next?
steps: Ask where exactly (site) and when it started (onset).
Ask what it feels like (character), whether it spreads (radiation) and how bad it is (severity).
Ask what makes it better or worse, and other symptoms such as vomiting or fever.
example.a: Use SOCRATES: site, onset, character, radiation, associated symptoms, timing, what changes it, severity

analogies.home: A detective asks open questions first, then checks details.
analogies.tech: A technician asks what you were doing when the app crashed.
analogies.sport: A coach asks what you felt before the injury.
analogies.farm: A vet asks the farmer how the animal has been eating and moving.

stages.mnemonic: SOCRATES for pain, and always ask about Allergies and Medicines before you act.
terms: The main problem that brings the patient in.
Illnesses and operations the patient has had before.
A question that invites a full answer, like 'Tell me more'.
Home, work, habits and support that affect health.

misc.wrong: A good history is a list of yes/no questions.
misc.right: Start with open questions and listen. Use closed questions to fill gaps.

stages.limits: The order and the checklists differ between schools and countries. They are memory aids, not rules.

stages.title: Physical examination concepts
stages.hook: Doctors use four basic skills on a body: look, feel, tap and listen. What could each one tell you?
explain: A physical examination checks the body for signs. The classic steps are inspection (looking), palpation (feeling with the hands), percussion (tapping to hear the sound) and auscultation (listening, usually with a stethoscope). Good order is wash hands, introduce yourself, ask permission, expose only what is needed, and keep dignity.

Start with a general look: does the patient look well or unwell? Colour, breathing, alertness, hydration. Then examine the relevant system, such as the heart and lungs for chest symptoms or the abdomen for tummy pain. Compare both sides when you can.
Examination findings never stand alone. They are combined with the history and tests. Always explain what you are doing, ask about pain before pressing and stop if the patient asks.

example.q: A fictional patient has tummy pain. Why does the examiner look first and press last?
steps: Looking (inspection) causes no discomfort.
Pressing a painful area first could make the patient tense and hide other signs.
So inspect, listen if relevant, then palpate gently, saving the sorest area for last.
example.a: Inspect first and palpate the tender area last to avoid causing needless pain

analogies.farm: A farmer taps a melon to hear if it is ripe, similar to percussion.
analogies.tech: A technician looks for lights, tests buttons and listens for fan noise.

Listening to body sounds, often with a stethoscope.

misc.wrong: The examination alone gives the diagnosis.
misc.right: Findings must be combined with the history and tests.

stages.title: Vital signs
stages.hook: Five numbers can quickly tell a nurse whether a patient is stable or in trouble. What are they?
explain: Vital signs are basic measurements of how the body is working: heart rate (pulse), respiratory rate (breaths per minute), blood pressure, temperature and oxygen saturation. Level of consciousness and pain are often added.

Typical resting adult ranges used in this game: heart rate 60 to 100 beats per minute; respiratory rate 12 to 20 breaths per minute; temperature about 36.5 to 37.5 °C; oxygen saturation 95 to 100 percent on room air; blood pressure about 90/60 to 120/80 mmHg for healthy adults, with the top number the systolic and the bottom the diastolic.

Children have different ranges: a resting heart rate and breathing rate are higher in babies than in adults. A single reading matters less than the trend and the patient's overall look. Early warning scores combine several vital signs to spot worsening early.

example.q: A fictional adult has HR 130, RR 28, BP 85/50 and temperature 39 °C. How should a junior act?
steps: HR above 100, RR above 20 and low BP are abnormal.
Fast heart, fast breathing, low BP and fever together suggest a very unwell patient (for example serious infection).
This needs urgent senior review and treatment.
example.a: Treat it as urgent and escalate immediately

analogies.home: A car dashboard shows speed, fuel and engine heat. Vital signs are the body's dashboard.
analogies.sport: A coach checks pulse and breathing during training.
analogies.sea: A ship's captain checks depth, speed and engine temperature.
analogies.tech: A server monitor shows load, memory and heat.

stages.mnemonic: HR, RR, BP, Temp, SpO₂: pulse, breaths, pressure, heat, oxygen.
terms: Heartbeats per minute; adult resting 60 to 100.
Breaths per minute; adult resting 12 to 20.
The force of blood on artery walls, written systolic over diastolic.
The percentage of haemoglobin carrying oxygen; usually 95 to 100 percent.

misc.wrong: A number outside the range always means disease.
misc.right: Athletes can have low resting heart rates, and anxiety can raise readings. Look at the trend and the patient.

stages.limits: Ranges here are simplified for healthy adults and vary with age, medicines, pregnancy and long-term conditions. Real thresholds come from local guidelines.

stages.title: Cardiovascular medicine
stages.hook: The heart beats about 100,000 times a day without a rest. What happens when the supply to the heart itself is blocked?
explain: The heart is a muscular pump with four chambers: two atria on top and two ventricles below. The right side sends blood to the lungs to pick up oxygen; the left side pumps oxygen-rich blood to the body. Valves keep blood flowing one way, and the lub-dub sound is the valves closing.

Arteries carry blood away from the heart under pressure, veins return it, and tiny capillaries let oxygen and nutrients pass into tissues. The heart muscle needs its own blood supply from the coronary arteries.

If a coronary artery is blocked, heart muscle can be damaged: a heart attack (myocardial infarction). Typical warning symptoms are chest pressure or pain, sometimes spreading to the arm or jaw, with sweating or breathlessness, though some people, especially women, older people and those with diabetes, may have milder or unusual symptoms. High blood pressure, smoking, high cholesterol, diabetes and inactivity raise the risk. Chest pain with these features is an emergency.

example.q: Trace the path of blood from the body back to the body, naming the main steps.
steps: Oxygen-poor blood returns to the right side of the heart.
The right ventricle pumps it to the lungs, where it picks up oxygen.
Oxygen-rich blood returns to the left side, and the left ventricle pumps it to the body.
example.a: Body → right heart → lungs → left heart → body

analogies.city: The heart is a pumping station and the vessels are pipes with one-way gates.
analogies.farm: A farm pump moves water along pipes to the fields; the heart moves blood to tissues.
analogies.home: A central heating pump pushes hot water round radiators.
analogies.tech: A cooling system pumps liquid around a computer.

stages.mnemonic: Right side to the lungs, left side to the life: right = lungs, left = body.
terms: A top chamber of the heart that receives blood.
A lower chamber of the heart that pumps blood out.
A vessel that carries blood away from the heart.
Heart muscle damage caused by a blocked blood supply; a heart attack.

misc.wrong: A heart attack always feels like crushing pain in the left chest.
misc.right: Symptoms can be mild or unusual, so possible heart attack symptoms need urgent assessment.

stages.limits: The simulation uses simplified anatomy and typical symptom patterns. Real assessments use ECGs and blood tests.

stages.title: Respiratory medicine
stages.hook: You breathe about 20,000 times a day. How does oxygen get from the air into your blood?
explain: Air enters through the nose and mouth, passes down the trachea (windpipe), splits into two bronchi and branches into smaller bronchioles. At the ends are millions of tiny air sacs called alveoli, surrounded by capillaries. Oxygen passes from the alveoli into the blood and carbon dioxide passes out. This swapping is gas exchange.
Breathing is driven by the diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle below the lungs. When it contracts and flattens, the chest expands, pressure falls and air flows in. When it relaxes, air flows out.

Common problems include asthma (airways narrow and swell, causing wheeze, cough and breathlessness), pneumonia (infection of the lung tissue) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (long-term airflow limitation, often linked to smoking). Severe difficulty speaking in full sentences, blue lips, confusion or very fast breathing are emergencies.

example.q: A fictional teen with asthma has a wheeze and cannot finish sentences. What does this suggest?
steps: Wheeze means narrowed airways.
Unable to finish sentences means breathing is severely limited.
This is a severe attack and needs urgent help.
example.a: A severe, urgent breathing problem needing immediate help

analogies.sea: A diver's tank supplies air; lungs bring oxygen from the air we breathe.

stages.mnemonic: Nose, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli: air goes down the tree to the leaves.

stages.title: Digestive and renal medicine
stages.hook: After a meal, food takes hours to travel through you. Meanwhile your kidneys quietly clean your blood. How do the two systems work?
explain: Digestion breaks food into small molecules that can be absorbed. It begins in the mouth with chewing and saliva, continues in the stomach, which mixes food with acid and enzymes, and is completed in the small intestine, where most nutrients are absorbed. The liver makes bile to help digest fats, and the pancreas releases digestive enzymes. The large intestine absorbs water and forms stool.

The kidneys are two bean-shaped organs that filter blood. They remove waste and extra water as urine, balance salts and help control blood pressure. Urine travels through the ureters to the bladder and out through the urethra.

Common problems include gastroenteritis (infection causing vomiting and diarrhoea, with risk of dehydration), reflux, ulcers and urinary tract infections. Warning signs include blood in vomit or stool, severe constant tummy pain, very little urine or signs of dehydration, especially in babies and older adults.

example.q: Why can severe diarrhoea be dangerous for a baby?
steps: Diarrhoea loses a lot of water and salts.
Babies have small reserves.
Dehydration develops fast, so early medical review is needed.
example.a: Fast fluid and salt loss can cause dangerous dehydration

analogies.home: A kitchen blender breaks food up; the stomach churns it.
analogies.farm: A farm sieve separates grain from husk; kidneys filter waste from blood.
analogies.city: A water treatment plant cleans water; kidneys clean blood.
analogies.tech: A spam filter keeps the good and removes the bad; the kidneys do similar for blood.

stages.mnemonic: Mouth, stomach, small intestine absorbs, large intestine dries. Kidneys filter, bladder stores.
terms: Breaking food into small parts the body can absorb.
The long tube where most nutrients are absorbed.
An organ that filters blood and makes urine.
Too little water in the body.

misc.wrong: Most digestion happens in the stomach.
misc.right: The stomach starts digestion, but most digestion and absorption happens in the small intestine.

trip.prompt: Trace food from mouth to the large intestine and note where nutrients are absorbed.

questions.q: Where is most nutrient absorption?
questions.why: The small intestine has a large surface for absorption.

questions.q: What do kidneys do?
o: Pump blood round the whole body
questions.why: Kidneys filter waste and water from blood.

questions.q: Order the path of urine.
questions.why: Urine flows from kidney to outside.

questions.q: What does bile help digest?
questions.why: Bile from the liver breaks fats into small droplets.

questions.q: What does the large intestine mainly absorb?
questions.why: It absorbs water, leaving stool.

questions.q: Match the organ to its role.
questions.why: Several organs cooperate in digestion and waste removal.

questions.q: A fictional baby has many watery stools, a dry mouth and very few wet nappies. What is the concern?
o: Too much sleep and a quiet mood
Overfeeding only, which needs no review
Normal baby behaviour at that age
questions.why: These are signs of dehydration.

questions.q: Vomiting blood is a red flag because it may mean...
o: A common cold in the throat and nose
Too little salt in the diet
questions.why: It needs urgent assessment.

questions.q: A person passes very little urine for a day and feels dizzy. What is the most useful thought?
o: They may be dehydrated or have a kidney problem and need assessment
Everything is normal and no action is needed
They need only a snack and a rest
It means their digestion is perfect today
questions.why: Low urine output is a warning.

questions.q: Why is the small intestine well designed for absorption?
questions.model: It is long and folded with tiny villi, giving a very large surface, and its thin walls sit next to blood vessels so nutrients pass into the blood quickly.
questions.why: Large surface and close blood supply.

panel.q: A fictional patient with severe constant right-lower tummy pain, fever and vomiting. What should the junior do?
o: Escalate to a senior for urgent assessment
Send home with reassurance and no further review
Wait a week and see how it goes
Ask only about diet and then discharge
panel.why: Severe persistent pain with fever needs urgent review for causes such as appendicitis.

panel.q: Why does a urinary infection sometimes cause back pain and fever when the kidneys are involved?
o: Infection can spread up to the kidneys and trigger inflammation
The bladder moves up the back during illness
The bones of the spine fuse together
The food they ate is poisoned
panel.why: Kidney infection is more serious than bladder infection.

panel.q: Why do the kidneys matter for blood pressure and body water?
panel.model: The kidneys regulate how much water and salt are kept or removed in urine, which affects blood volume and so blood pressure.
panel.why: Kidneys balance fluid and salts.

teach.model: Digestion breaks food into small parts that are absorbed, mostly in the small intestine. The kidneys filter the blood to remove waste and extra water as urine, and help balance body water.

stages.title: Nervous and endocrine systems
stages.hook: Touch a hot pan and your hand jumps before you feel pain. Meanwhile, hormones change your mood and growth over years. How do two control systems differ?
explain: The nervous system is made of the brain, spinal cord and nerves. Nerve cells (neurons) carry electrical signals very fast. Sensory nerves bring information in, the brain and spinal cord process it, and motor nerves send commands to muscles. A reflex, such as pulling away from heat, uses a short pathway through the spinal cord and so is quick.

The endocrine system uses glands that release hormones into the blood. Hormones act more slowly but for longer. Examples: insulin from the pancreas lowers blood glucose; thyroid hormones set the pace of metabolism; adrenaline prepares the body for action; growth hormone helps growth.

Diabetes is when blood glucose stays too high because the body lacks insulin or does not respond to it properly. Signs include thirst, passing a lot of urine and tiredness. A stroke is when blood supply to part of the brain is cut off; sudden face drooping, arm weakness and slurred speech are emergency signs (the FAST check: face, arms, speech, time).

example.q: A fictional patient has a drooping face, weak arm and slurred speech that started 20 minutes ago. What do you do?
steps: These are classic signs of stroke (FAST: face, arm, speech).
Time matters because brain cells die without blood.
Call emergency help and note the time symptoms started.
example.a: Treat as an emergency, call for help and note the time of onset

analogies.tech: Nerves are like fast cables; hormones are like postal letters that arrive later but last.
analogies.city: Phone calls are quick (nerves) while newspapers reach everyone more slowly (hormones).
analogies.home: A light switch is instant; a heating timer changes things slowly.
analogies.sport: A coach shouts an instant instruction (nerve) or sets a season plan (hormone).

stages.mnemonic: Nerves = fast and short, hormones = slow and long. FAST for stroke.
terms: A nerve cell that carries electrical signals.
A fast automatic reaction that uses a short pathway.
A chemical messenger released into the blood by a gland.
A hormone that lowers blood glucose.

misc.wrong: Diabetes only happens from eating too much sugar.
misc.right: Diabetes comes from problems with insulin. Type 1 is an immune condition, and type 2 is linked to many factors including genetics, weight and activity.

stages.limits: This stage simplifies types of diabetes and the many hormones involved.

trip.prompt: Compare the nervous system with the endocrine system in a table.

questions.q: What does a neuron do?
questions.why: Neurons are nerve cells.

questions.q: Which hormone lowers blood glucose?
questions.why: Insulin helps cells take up glucose.

questions.q: Which is quicker?
questions.why: Nerve signals act within milliseconds.

questions.q: What is a reflex?
o: A hormone made in the gland
questions.why: Reflexes use a short pathway.

questions.q: Order the pathway of a reflex.
questions.why: A short loop makes it fast.

questions.q: Match the hormone to its job.
questions.why: Each hormone has a target effect.

questions.q: A fictional person has face drooping and slurred speech. What does FAST suggest?
o: A common cold in the head
questions.why: Face, arm, speech, time.

questions.q: Why does a stroke need rapid treatment?
o: It is boring to leave it waiting
The brain is large, so it is slow
questions.why: Time lost is brain lost.

questions.q: A fictional teen is very thirsty, urinating often and losing weight. What is a likely thought?
o: High blood glucose such as diabetes, needing testing
Too little water drunk, and nothing else
A broken bone in the leg
An excess of vitamins in the diet
questions.why: These are classic symptoms of high glucose.

questions.q: Compare the nervous and endocrine systems in speed and duration.
questions.model: The nervous system uses electrical signals that act very fast and briefly, while the endocrine system uses hormones in the blood that act more slowly but last longer.
questions.why: They complement each other.

panel.q: A person with diabetes feels shaky, sweaty and confused. Which explanation should be considered urgently?
o: Too much sleep the night before
A normal reflex of the body
panel.why: Hypoglycaemia is an emergency that a clinician must check.

panel.q: A fictional patient had stroke-like symptoms that went away in ten minutes. Why still seek urgent assessment?
o: It may be a warning of a later stroke
It cannot matter if symptoms went away
It was a reflex and nothing more
panel.why: A transient ischaemic attack is a warning sign.

panel.q: Why might the body use both nerves and hormones to control things?
panel.model: Nerves give immediate short responses, such as pulling away from heat, while hormones give slower longer-lasting control, such as growth and blood sugar.
panel.why: Different tasks need different speeds.

teach.model: Nerves carry fast electrical signals from the brain and spinal cord to the body. Hormones are chemical messengers in the blood that act more slowly but for longer. Insulin is a hormone that lowers blood sugar.

stages.title: Introduction to laboratory investigations
stages.hook: A drop of blood can reveal anaemia, infection or high sugar. How do doctors pick which tests to order?
explain: Laboratory tests measure things in blood, urine or other samples to help answer a question raised by the history and examination. Common ones are a full blood count (red cells, white cells, platelets, haemoglobin), urea and electrolytes and creatinine (kidney function and salts), glucose, liver tests and cultures that grow germs.

Tests are chosen for a reason. A good question is: how would the result change what I do? Needless tests cost money, cause discomfort and can produce false alarms. Every test has limits: sensitivity (how well it finds people who have the condition) and specificity (how well it says no for those who do not). No test is perfect.

Results are compared with a reference range, the interval in which most healthy people fall (usually the middle 95 percent). A value just outside the range may not be disease, and a value inside may not exclude it. Samples must be labelled correctly with the right patient, because a mix-up can cause harm.

example.q: A fictional adult feels tired and looks pale. Which first blood test would help?
steps: Tiredness and paleness suggest anaemia.
A full blood count measures haemoglobin.
A low haemoglobin would support anaemia; further tests would find the cause.

analogies.home: A smoke test checks whether a pipe is leaking, but you only do it if you suspect a leak.
analogies.farm: A farmer tests soil before choosing a fertiliser.
analogies.tech: A diagnostic program checks specific parts.
analogies.sport: A coach takes timings only if they answer a question.

stages.mnemonic: Right test, right patient, right reason, right label.
terms: A test counting red cells, white cells and platelets and measuring haemoglobin.
The interval in which most healthy people's results fall.
How well a test finds people who truly have the condition.
How well a test rules out people who do not have the condition.

misc.wrong: A normal test result proves nothing is wrong.
misc.right: Tests can miss disease, especially early. Doctors combine results with the history, examination and the trend.

stages.limits: Reference ranges differ between laboratories, ages and sexes. This stage gives only general ideas, not values for real patients.

trip.prompt: Find what each part of the blood count measures.

questions.q: A full blood count measures...
questions.why: It counts red cells, white cells and platelets and measures haemoglobin.

questions.q: Why should a doctor ask 'how will this result change what I do'?
o: To order as many more tests as possible
To delay care until more is known
To confuse patients with long questions
questions.why: Tests should be purposeful.

questions.q: A reference range describes...
o: Where most healthy people's results fall
The price of a test in the laboratory shop
The age of the laboratory machine
A treatment dose for all adults
questions.why: It is the usual healthy interval.

questions.q: A test with high sensitivity is good at...
o: Finding people who have the condition
Ruling out people who are free of it only
Being cheap enough for every clinic
Being quick enough to read at once
questions.why: Sensitivity is the true positive rate.

questions.q: A result is slightly outside the reference range but the patient is well. What is the best thought?
o: It may not be disease and may need repeating
It is always serious and needs treatment straight away
Ignore it forever and never recheck
questions.why: About 5 percent of healthy people fall outside a 95 percent range.

questions.q: Match the test to what it helps assess.
questions.why: Tests answer specific questions.

questions.q: Order the testing process.
items: Result is interpreted with the patient's story
questions.why: A test is part of a reasoning loop.

questions.q: A sample is labelled with the wrong patient's name. What is the risk?
o: Someone may get the wrong treatment
None, as long as the tube looks full
questions.why: Mislabelling is a serious safety error.

questions.q: A very concerning result comes back (for example a very low haemoglobin) for a fictional patient. What should the junior do?
o: Act promptly and tell a senior
Wait a week before telling anyone
File it away with the other results
Delete it in case it is a mistake
questions.why: Critical results need quick escalation.

questions.q: Why can a normal test still be consistent with disease?
questions.model: No test is perfect: it may be done too early or miss the condition, so a normal result does not fully rule out disease.
questions.why: Tests have limits.

panel.q: A doctor orders twenty tests for a patient with a mild headache. What is a concern?
o: Unnecessary tests may cause false alarms and harm
More tests always help and never harm
Tests are free, so there is no concern
Doctors need practice ordering many tests
panel.why: Over-testing leads to false positives and extra procedures.

panel.q: Why are reference ranges for children different from adults?
o: The machines are different for children
panel.why: Normal values depend on age.

panel.q: Explain the difference between sensitivity and specificity in plain words.
panel.model: Sensitivity is how well a test finds people who have the condition; specificity is how well it correctly says no for people who do not.
panel.why: Two different strengths of a test.

teach.topic: Why and how we order tests
teach.model: Tests answer questions raised by the history and examination. A test is useful if the result changes what we do. Results are compared with a reference range, and no test is perfect.

points.ask: How do we read the result?
